architecturalDifferenceFromFile1.file1Pattern: ONE server instance, created once in section B, reused across sections C/G/H, closed exactly once at the very end of main().
architecturalDifferenceFromFile1.file2Pattern: TWO independent server instances ("server" in section C, "server2" in section E), each created AND closed inline within its own section during normal execution -- NOT reused across sections and NOT deferred to the end. Each was originally closed via a bare fire-and-forget `.close()` call with no callback/await/verification.
architecturalDifferenceFromFile1.riskInOriginalCode: If an exception occurred between a section's server creation and its own inline .close() call, that server would remain open for the rest of the process, and the original main().catch() handler (unlike file 1's) never called process.exit() or closed any server -- meaning an exception mid-section could leave the process hanging indefinitely (an open http.Server keeps Node's event loop alive). This was a pre-existing latent bug that Stage 3A's centralized cleanup now fixes as a side effect.
architecturalDifferenceFromFile1.designDecision: Rather than removing the inline closes (which would leave both servers listening for the remainder of main()'s execution, sections D-L, harmlessly but unnecessarily), the inline closes were KEPT as the fast/normal path, and BOTH servers were additionally hoisted to module scope and wired into the outer runEntry() finally as an exception-path safety net. closeHttpServerBounded() treats an already-closed server (server.listening === false) as a safe no-op, so calling it again in the finally after a normal inline close is harmless.

sharedHelperDecision.coreAlgorithmIdentical: The bounded-close ALGORITHM (race close-completion against a resolving timeout, force-close via closeAllConnections() on timeout, re-await the original close promise, clear the timer in a real finally covering every path) is identical between file 1's single server and file 2's two servers -- there was no reason to write it twice.
sharedHelperDecision.extractedTo: scripts/lib/qa-temp-db.js exports closeHttpServerBounded(server, timeoutMs), additive (no existing export changed). File 1 was refactored to call the shared version instead of its own local copy (re-verified: still 82/82 assert calls identical after that refactor).
sharedHelperDecision.file2SpecificAddition: closeHttpServerBounded() also checks `server.listening === false` and returns immediately as a safe no-op -- needed for file 2's already-closed-by-inline-call case, which file 1 never encountered (its server is only ever closed once, in the outer finally). This check is harmless for file 1 too.
sharedHelperDecision.whatWasNotShared: The overall runEntry()/cleanup-step wiring (which servers exist, DB handle close, root cleanup ordering) remains file-specific, since file 2 has two servers and a different normal-vs-exception-path closing pattern -- only the single-server bounded-close primitive itself was extracted.

requireCacheEvictionSearch.method: grep for require.cache and delete require.cache across the entire file

objectIdentityReasoningChain: 1. Node.js require() resolves relative/computed paths to a canonical absolute path BEFORE consulting require.cache.

2. require.resolve() run directly against all 3 call sites (this file's own require, and the internal requires inside routes/settings.js and routes/geo-live.js) all produced the exact same absolute path: /home/claude/restore_work/work/utils/db.js.

3. No delete require.cache[...] or equivalent cache-eviction call exists anywhere in this file (confirmed by grep, 0 matches) -- so the module cache entry for that absolute path, once populated by the FIRST require, is never invalidated for the remainder of the process.

4. utils/db.js exports getDb (and initDb), and internally guards DB creation with `if (wrappedDb) return wrappedDb;` -- so even multiple getDb() calls across the 3 requiring sites return the SAME wrapped DB object reference, not new ones.

5. Conclusion: exactly ONE DB handle object exists for the entire lifetime of this test run. The single module-scope `dbHandle` variable (assigned once, from this file's own getDb() call) is a complete and sufficient reference for cleanup -- closing it via db._db.close() releases the one and only underlying sql.js WASM object that routes/settings.js and routes/geo-live.js also transitively hold references to (since they hold the SAME object, not copies).

generationAndRetryStateMachine.reason: Two real boundary cases in the concurrent-close state machine were audited and fixed: (1) a server closed then re-listen()'d would previously hit the stale completed state and no-op, leaking the re-listened server; (2) a failed original close would previously be marked completed anyway, permanently blocking any retry.
generationAndRetryStateMachine.completedOnlyAfterActualClose: state is marked completed based on the ORIGINAL close promise genuinely resolving, not on closeAllConnections() succeeding and not unconditionally in a finally
generationAndRetryStateMachine.concurrentFailureShared: two concurrent callers on an attempt that ultimately fails both receive the identical rejection (same Error object), proven via HTTPCLOSE13 with Promise.allSettled
generationAndRetryStateMachine.bugFoundDuringTestDesign: Initial versions of HTTPCLOSE11/12 had bugs in the TEST setup itself (double-wrapping server.close on re-listen; a mock that let the real close succeed while only faking an error report to the helper, which made a "failed" first attempt actually already-closed by the time of the second call). Both were caught by 2 real test failures (not silently passed), diagnosed, and fixed in the test code -- the underlying helper implementation was correct throughout; the tests needed fixing to correctly exercise it.
